title: Tunnel Vision in a Busy Clinic

patient.name: Mdm Goh Lai Heng
patient.presenting_complaint: Came alone by taxi for her glaucoma review; has severe tunnel vision and is unsure of the clinic layout

history.hpc: Mdm Goh has advanced glaucoma with severe constriction of her side vision. She came alone today. She says: 'I can only see a bit in the middle, the side all dark, so I walk slowly slowly, scared knock into things.' She finds the busy clinic with chairs and other patients hard to navigate. No new symptoms, here for routine review.
history.pmhx: Advanced primary open-angle glaucoma, both eyes. Osteoarthritis of the knees.
medications: Latanoprost eye drops ON both eyes
Timolol eye drops BD both eyes
history.social_hx: Lives alone, manages with help from a neighbour. Came alone by taxi today.

examination_findings.anterior_segment: Normal anterior segments; optic discs show advanced glaucomatous cupping (known)
examination_findings.fundus: Known advanced glaucomatous optic neuropathy, for doctor review

investigations.fall_risk_assessment: High risk: elderly, severe peripheral field loss (tunnel vision) making navigation hazardous, osteoarthritis affecting mobility, and currently unaccompanied in a busy environment.
investigations.va_distance: RE 6/12, LE 6/18 (central acuity relatively preserved despite severe field loss).

diagnosis: High fall risk driven mainly by severe visual field loss rather than central acuity — a patient can have 'good' central VA yet be at high risk because of tunnel vision. Active guidance and a safe path through the clinic are needed.

immediate: Recognise that good central VA does not exclude high fall risk when peripheral field is severely constricted
Personally guide the patient through the clinic, describing obstacles and offering an arm to hold
Seat her in a clear, well-lit spot with a direct, unobstructed path, away from clutter
Keep walkways near her clear of bags, chairs, and equipment
Accompany her for each move (to testing, to the doctor, to the exit) rather than letting her navigate alone
Document the fall risk assessment and the actions taken (guided, seated safely, escorted)
follow_up: Doctor to review glaucoma control and visual fields
Arrange for a volunteer or staff escort to the taxi at the end of the visit
Encourage her to attend future visits with a companion and flag this in her records
patient_education: Acknowledge her own caution and reassure her that staff will guide her
Explain that her side vision loss makes busy areas risky, so she should ask for help to move around
Advise her to keep taking her glaucoma drops as prescribed to protect remaining vision
Encourage bringing a companion and arranging escort help for appointments

key_points: Establishes the severe peripheral field loss and difficulty navigating
Confirms she came alone and has mobility-affecting comorbidity (knee osteoarthritis)
Recognises her own safety strategy (walking slowly) as a clue to high risk
Confirms she is here for routine glaucoma review with no new symptoms
Performs and documents a fall risk assessment at this visit
Identifies field loss (tunnel vision) as the dominant risk factor despite fair central VA
Notes the unaccompanied status and busy environment as added risks
Recognises that central acuity alone does not determine fall risk
Classifies the patient as high fall risk due to severe field loss
Understands the clinic environment contributes to the risk
Knows high risk requires active guidance, not just documentation
Personally guides and escorts the patient and offers an arm to hold
Seats her safely with a clear path and keeps walkways uncluttered
Documents the assessment and actions taken
Arranges escort to the taxi and flags the need for a companion at future visits
